"You're taking mine away."
"No. I'm asking for a family plan. Mine included."
She looked up. "Yours, Papa?"
"I check work emails in bed and I wake up grumpy. You've seen it."

"Eleven on weekends?"

"Then you do the dishes."
"Deal. And you?"

I'm Farhan, and I'll admit my first try was a disaster. I found Afreen, my fifteen-year-old, on her phone at one in the morning and simply took it away for a week. She stopped talking to me. She borrowed her friend's old phone instead. My own phone, of course, stayed on my pillow.
After a week of cold dinners, I sat down with her and said, "I got that wrong." I explained what I'd read about light and sleep, and asked what she thought was fair. She suggested a basket by the front door. She added, "Yours too, Abbu."
Now we both drop our phones there at ten. Some nights she grumbles. But she's less tired, and honestly, so am I.

Family meeting note, Sunday
As his mother, I had been snatching Divyansh's phone at midnight and we'd end up shouting. Tonight we tried a meeting instead. I explained why I worry: he's been falling asleep in class, and I read how screens keep brains awake. Divyansh said the grabbing felt like punishment, and that his dad and I scroll in bed too. Fair point. So we agreed together: all phones, including ours, charge on the hall shelf from ten-thirty on school nights. Weekends, eleven-thirty. Divyansh chose the times with us. Three nights in, there has been no fight. He even reminded his dad to hand his phone over.
Keerthana

Tuesday night
We had the phone talk with Sharmila tonight. As her father, my instinct was to lay down the law, but I remembered how that went last time: door slammed, three days of silence. So this time I started with why. I told her I've seen her tired and tearful in the mornings, and that I read screens at night keep the brain awake. I asked what she thought a fair rule was. She said, 'Ten o'clock, but only if you do it too, Papa. You watch cricket clips till midnight.' Ouch. True. So all phones charge in the kitchen from ten. It's 10:15 now and I'm writing this on paper, not my phone. Sharmila just knocked to say goodnight, smiling.
Jagdish

In their house above the cloth shop in Kasganj, phone rules used to be shouted. Parul would snatch her daughter Noor's phone at eleven, Noor would slam the door, and nobody slept well. One Sunday after lunch, Parul put a basket on the table. "I'm tired of fighting," she said. "I check shop orders in bed till midnight too, and I wake up with a headache. What if every phone sleeps in this basket from ten, mine included?"
Noor narrowed her eyes. "Yours too? Even when suppliers text?"
"Even then. They can wait till morning."
Noor asked for Saturdays till eleven, and Parul agreed. In the first week Parul slipped once, and Noor pointed at the basket, grinning. Parul put her phone in without a word.
